chunks: And as for what was narrated - Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Abi al-Subbah from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him about a man who makes a vow to God to fast a specific named day, he said: 'He must fast it always, both in residence and during travel.'

The ruling regarding it is that if he stipulates upon himself to fast it during travel and residence, and this is the third category among the categories we presented earlier, and that which indicates this is what was narrated: -(689) 64 - Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Abd Allah ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar who said: Bundar, the freedman of Idris, wrote: 'O my master, I vowed to fast every Saturday. If I do not fast it, what expiation is obligatory upon me?' He (peace be upon him) wrote: 'And I read it: Do not leave it except due to an excuse, and fasting it is not obligatory upon you during travel or illness, unless you intended that. If you broke it without an excuse, then give charity equivalent to each day to seven poor people. We ask God for success in what He loves and is pleased with.'

As for voluntary fasting during travel, it is disliked (makruh), and that which indicates this is what we presented earlier regarding the prohibition of fasting during travel, and that is general for voluntary and obligatory fasting, and that which adds clarification to this is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for breaking a vow to fast a specific day without a valid excuse?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the juristic distinction between general and specific vows (*nadhr*) regarding fasting, establishing that a general vow to fast a specific day binds the individual regardless of travel or illness. It highlights the practical application of this ruling through the correspondence of Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to Bundar, specifying that while voluntary fasting during travel is *makruh*, breaking a vow without valid excuse requires expiation (*kaffarah*) in the form of feeding seven poor people. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the precise conditions of vows and the flexibility granted to travelers while maintaining the sanctity of personal commitments.
